title: Man killed by Transit Police in Surrey identified as 23-year-old Hazelton resident
subtitle: A man shot by the Transit Police in Surrey on the weekend has been identified as Naverone Christian Landon Woods.
article: When Naverone Christian Landon Woods headed to Vancouver for his uncle's funeral in early December, his family didn't worry.
They knew he loved the big-city lifestyle and would eventually return to his tiny hometown village of Hazelton, B.C., for a visit sooner or later.
What they didn't expect was to see Woods, 23, on the TV news, a day after he was shot by Transit police at a Surrey Safeway store at 104th Avenue and King George Boulevard.
He died later in hospital.

"It shocked me because none of the family knew," said Ed Patsey, the oldest of Woods' seven stepbrothers. "I was watching the news and I seen it and I knew it was my brother then and there. No one phoned us and told the family he'd been shot, or nothing.
"That's what I'm ticked off about."
The phones started ringing, in Hazelton and Vancouver, where Woods had planned to spend Christmas with his cousins, to find out what had happened.
It appears Woods has been staying with a girlfriend in Surrey, Patsey said, when the tragic incident occurred on Sunday, Dec. 28.
Transit police say they received a call early that morning that a man had gone behind the counter of a convenience store just 300 metres from the Surrey Central SkyTrain station and demanded a knife.
They then heard about a disturbance inside the nearby Safeway and headed to the grocery store where they found Woods with a knife.
According to the Transit police, Woods was shot after he refused to drop the knife and moved toward officers.
Investigators with the Independent Investigations Office continue to look into the incident.

His family say the situation was out of character for Woods, who was described as a gentle, quiet guy who had no history of mental illness. And although he liked to party with his cousins on a weekend, Patsey said his brother didn't go out every night.
"I feel so bad about his," Woods' aunt Valerie Simms-Muldoe said. "There was no need for it. He wasn't out to hurt anybody."

Born in the middle of 11 siblings - the oldest, Patsey, is 40, the youngest 12 - Woods spent some time in Terrace with his mother before living for few years with his father and other step-siblings in Hazelton, a small town located at the junction of the Bulkley and Skeena Rivers in northern B.C.

He grew up playing basketball and ice-hockey like his father, Patsey said. Although quiet, Woods had a lot of friends and liked to have fun. Patsey recalls one incident when Woods, playing goal, slicked back his dark curls to look like former Canucks goalie Roberto Luongo, and got a ribbing from his friends.
But that didn't bother Woods, who had longed for the big city lifestyle and often stayed for long periods of time at the Coast with his cousins and other relatives.
"He was a quiet guy and very nice," said family friend Philip Stewart. "He had a lot going for him. It was shocking to see what happened."
Patsey said his brother had been working construction in Vancouver and picking up other odd jobs, but would return to Hazelton a few times a year to see family.
"He liked to come home but then he'd get homesick and want to go back to Vancouver again," he said. "In a small town like this there is not much to do here."

The family is hoping Woods' body will be flown back to Smithers on Friday so they can start planning the celebration of life and ceremonial feast, which will likely involve the entire community of 300.
"It's still pretty tough. It's going to be even tougher when we bring him back on Friday," Patsey said. "He was a great kid, he will be missed by everyone around here."
